intro: Somebody decided where the stop sign on your corner would go. Somebody decided how many days a year your school is open. Somebody decided that a police officer needs a good reason before searching your backpack. Those somebodies are not far away. Some of them meet in a brick building in your town. Some meet under a silver dome in Springfield. Some meet in Washington, D.C. And every one of them got the job because voters put them there.

This unit is about how that works. You will meet the three levels of government, local, state and national, and the three branches at each level: the people who make laws, the people who carry them out, and the judges who decide what the laws mean. You will follow an idea as it turns into a bill and then into a law. You will see how an election works and why the word democracy means the people hold the power.

Then you will look at the other side of the deal. The Bill of Rights lists what the government can never take from you. In return, citizens owe the community some things: obeying laws, paying taxes, serving on juries, voting and speaking up. You will learn how four fourth graders got a crosswalk painted, and how two Chicago women, Jane Addams and Ida B. Wells, used their rights to make life fairer for thousands of people.
bigQuestion: Who holds the power in a democracy, and what does each person owe to the community in return?

timeline.t: Delegates in Philadelphia write the U.S. Constitution and set up three branches of government.
The states add the Bill of Rights, the first ten amendments, to the Constitution.
At Gettysburg, Lincoln describes government of the people, by the people, for the people.
Jane Addams and Ellen Gates Starr open Hull House on Halsted Street in Chicago.
Ida B. Wells begins printing the facts about lynching after three friends are killed in Memphis.
Illinois lets women vote for president; Wells founds the Alpha Suffrage Club in Chicago.
The Nineteenth Amendment gives women across the United States the right to vote.
Jane Addams becomes the first American woman to win the Nobel Peace Prize.
Illinois voters approve the state constitution still used today.
The Twenty-sixth Amendment lowers the voting age to eighteen across the nation.
Students count cars, sign petitions and speak at council meetings to change their own streets.

words.d: the group of people who make the rules for a community and see that they are followed
a rule made by a government that everyone in the community must follow
the branch that makes laws by voting; a council, the General Assembly, or Congress
the branch that carries out laws; led by a mayor, governor or president
the branch made of courts and judges
a written plan for a new law that has not been passed yet
when a governor or president refuses to sign a bill
a government where the people hold the power
a change added to the Constitution
something you are allowed to do or have that cannot be taken away without a very good reason
something you owe or must do, such as obeying laws and paying taxes
a written request to the government, often signed by many people

test.q: Which of these is a job of government?
choices: Running public schools and fixing roads
Choosing what a family watches on TV
Deciding which team wins a game
test.why: Governments build roads, run schools, keep parks open and pay police and firefighters.

test.q: A village board, the General Assembly and Congress are examples of which three levels?
test.why: A village board is local, the General Assembly is the state legislature, and Congress is national.

test.q: Who carries out the laws in Illinois?
test.why: The governor leads the state's executive branch, which carries out the laws.

test.q: What can the U.S. Supreme Court do if a law breaks the Constitution?
choices: Rule that the law cannot be used
test.why: The Supreme Court can strike down a law that goes against the Constitution.

test.q: What must happen before a bill reaches the governor in Illinois?
choices: Both the House and the Senate must pass the same words
The Supreme Court must approve it
test.why: A bill goes through committee and both houses of the General Assembly before the governor sees it.

test.q: How many U.S. senators does Illinois have?
test.why: Every state has two senators. Illinois sends seventeen members to the House.

test.q: Why does the United States use representative democracy instead of direct democracy?
choices: Because millions of people cannot all vote on every question
Because representatives do not need elections
test.why: Direct democracy works for a small group. A large nation chooses representatives to decide for it.

test.q: In the stop sign story, what did the village board do before voting?
choices: Listened to neighbors on both sides and asked questions
test.why: The board heard Mrs. Reyes and Mr. Kowalski, asked about car counts and cost, and then voted.

test.q: Which freedom lets a newspaper print a story that makes the mayor look bad?
test.why: Freedom of the press, in the First Amendment, protects reporters who print the truth.

test.q: In a fair trial, who has to prove something?
choices: The accused person must prove innocence
The jury must prove the judge is fair
test.why: A person is innocent until proven guilty. The government has to prove its case.

test.q: Which of these is a responsibility of a citizen?
choices: Serving on a jury when called
test.why: Jury duty is something citizens owe. Speech, religion and trials are rights the government owes them.

test.q: The current Illinois Constitution was written in which city and year?
test.why: Illinois has had four constitutions. The current one was written in 1970 and approved by voters.

test.q: What is the Illinois state tree?
test.why: The white oak is the state tree. The cardinal is the state bird and the violet the state flower.

test.q: In the crosswalk story, what did the four friends do after the council did not answer for a month?
choices: Wrote a polite note to follow up
test.why: Following up is part of making a change. Kim wrote to Ms. Duarte and learned the council had voted yes.

test.q: What did Ida B. Wells do after a mob destroyed her newspaper office?
choices: She moved to Springfield to become governor
She kept printing the facts and took her fight north
test.why: Wells could not return to Memphis, but she kept writing and later organized voters in Chicago.

write.prompt: Make a claim: Is voting or speaking up the more powerful tool for changing a community? Use evidence from the stop sign story, the crosswalk story, and the lives of Jane Addams or Ida B. Wells to support your claim.
tips: Claim: pick one tool, voting or speaking up, and say it clearly in your first sentence.
Evidence: use at least two examples from the unit, such as the board's four-to-two vote or the one hundred forty names on the petition.
Reasoning: explain why your evidence shows your tool worked. What would have happened without it?
The other side: say why someone might pick the other tool, then explain why you still think yours is stronger.
